title: Visvesvaraya Raises the KRS Dam
subtitle: How Mysore Turned the Kaveri into a Modern Sea
figure: M. Visvesvaraya and Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
era: KRS project, foundation 1911; dam built 1924; completion work to 1931
region: Kannambadi, Krishna Raja Sagara, Mandya, Mysore and the Kaveri basin
moral: A dam is strongest when imagination and public need hold together.

sources.citation: M. Visvesvaraya, Memoirs of My Working Life (1951)
sources.note: Primary account for the KRS project, opposition and engineering decisions.

sources.citation: Mysore Public Works Department KRS project records, 1911-1931
sources.note: Administrative and engineering records for construction.

sources.citation: Janaki Nair, Mysore Modern (University of Minnesota Press, 2011)
sources.note: Places KRS in the political economy of princely modernisation.

panels.shot: epic wide of the massive KRS dam with water stretching to the horizon and the silhouettes of Visvesvaraya and Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV in the foreground

dialogue.text: In Mysore’s age of experiments, M. Visvesvaraya and Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV dared to raise a sea from the Kaveri’s flow — and almost saw their dream washed away before it stood.

panels.shot: tight two-shot in a dim palace study, lamplight on maps and faces

dialogue.text: In 1911, in a quiet palace room far from the roar of the Kaveri, a young Maharaja and his Diwan traced a line on a map that would drown villages and feed cities.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot from behind Visvesvaraya looking down at the map dotted with canals and a dam-line

dialogue.speaker: M. Visvesvaraya
dialogue.text: Highness, one wall here can turn seasons of flood into years of grain.

panels.shot: medium shot of the Maharaja straightening in his chair, decision in his eyes

dialogue.text: Mysore was already called a ‘model state’, its ruler eager for schools, mills, and power. But a dam of this scale risked treasure, reputation, and the wrath of those downstream.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of the Kaveri at Kannambadi, wild and untamed, under monsoon clouds

dialogue.text: Down in the valley, the Kaveri had carved her own path for ages, rushing past Kannambadi’s fields, ignoring the earlier dream of Tipu, whose unbuilt dam lived only in memory and a plaque.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of a council table with British and Mysore officials around it

dialogue.text: The project had to cross not just a river, but a tangle of doubts, rival claims, and imperial caution. Could Mysore be trusted with so much water, so much concrete, so much risk?

panels.shot: close-up on Visvesvaraya’s face as he addresses unseen critics, jaw set

dialogue.speaker: M. Visvesvaraya
dialogue.text: We store floods, release measured flows, and share them by agreement. Without storage, all lose.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of the Maharaja signing the project sanction with a ceremonial pen

dialogue.text: In 1911, with a steady hand and a stroke of ink, the Maharaja approved a dam that would submerge Kannambadi and lift Mysore’s fortunes, binding his name to a wall yet to rise.

panels.shot: sweeping panoramic shot of early construction, with workers swarming over foundations

dialogue.text: By the early 1910s, Kannambadi was no longer only a village; it was a camp of surveyors, masons, and labourers, carving foundations into hard rock under a Diwan who believed order was also an engineering tool.

panels.shot: medium shot of Visvesvaraya examining a sample of surki mortar in his hand

dialogue.text: Cement was scarce and costly. The dam would stand on surki mortar—lime and brick dust—tested, retested, and arranged with such discipline that every joint became a calculation, not a guess.

panels.shot: detailed mid-shot of engineers around a scale model of the dam with crest gates

dialogue.text: On his drawing boards, the wall did more than block water. With automatic crest gates, it could lift itself in flood and fall in drought, turning the river’s moods into a measured, mechanical rhythm.

panels.shot: close-up of the actual crest gate mechanism installed on the partially built dam, gleaming in the sun

dialogue.text: These were not imported fantasies. They were practical, tested devices, building on Visvesvaraya’s earlier work, designed so that no inattentive human hand could delay crucial releases.

panels.shot: somber mid-wide of villagers watching as markings are placed on their soon-to-be-submerged homes

dialogue.text: Yet every foot the dam rose was a line higher on the walls of Kannambadi’s homes. Progress meant packing memories into bundles, watching fields measured not for harvest, but for depth.

panels.shot: intimate medium shot of the Maharaja and Visvesvaraya walking along the half-built dam at dusk

dialogue.speaker: Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
dialogue.text: We lift this state, Sir, yet we drown a village. Let us be worthy of both.

panels.shot: montage-like wide with superimposed sense of time passing: changing equipment, growing wall, different seasons

dialogue.text: War years, price shocks, and supply delays stretched the work. But stone by stone, season by season, the structure rose above the valley, until by 1924 its masonry bulk commanded the river.

panels.shot: grand wide shot of the reservoir beginning to fill, water creeping over former fields

dialogue.text: As sluices closed and gates took their positions, the old Kaveri narrowed and a new sheet of water began to spread, swallowing furrows and footpaths, birthing Krishna Raja Sagara, the sea of the Maharaja.

panels.shot: dynamic wide shot of irrigation canals carrying water into dry fields, farmers looking on

dialogue.text: From the reservoir’s edge, water ran in orderly lines, not wild floods but timed releases, turning Mandya’s soils into cane and paddy, and promising that drought would no longer be an annual guest.

panels.shot: medium shot of urban Mysore with a new water tower and pipes being laid

dialogue.text: Beyond the fields, pipes carried KRS water into Mysore’s taps, joining the dam to the city’s daily life—a hidden link between a palace decision, a rural valley, and a glass of drinking water.

panels.shot: close shot of a commemorative plaque at the dam site mentioning Tipu’s earlier intent and the present project

dialogue.text: Near the crest, stone letters recalled Tipu’s unfulfilled plan, linking past intent to present achievement, and quietly reminding visitors that history often moves by delayed dreams and different hands.

panels.shot: high-angle shot in the late 1920s of both men overlooking the fully formed lake and far-off green fields

dialogue.text: By the close of the 1920s and into the early 1930s, the KRS stood not only as masonry finished, gates adjusted, and canals refined, but as proof that a princely state could plan like a modern power.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on Visvesvaraya’s lined face, eyes reflecting both the water and the memory of resistance overcome

dialogue.text: The dam did not end scarcity, nor erase displacement. But it carved a path where imagination, calculation, and public need held together long enough to change a river’s fate—and ours.
